title: Compression vs Batching: Staircase Benchmark Snapshot
content:
Purpose
---
Quick exploratory benchmark to compare payload compression (gzip, brotli) applied to response chunks versus increasing batching depth (small, medium, large) for sessionized chat-style workloads. Focused on how these levers change observed percentiles (p50/p95/p99), end-to-end client-perceived latency, and $/1k tokens. This is a working sketch — not exhaustive, but captures surprising interactions for follow-up experiments.

Summary (top-line)
---
- Compression on response payloads reduces network transfer for long responses; latency wins are visible at p50 and p95 in high-bandwidth-limited scenarios but can worsen p99 when CPU contention exists on the host serving threads.
- Increasing batching depth (grouping requests) reduces per-token GPU time, cutting $/1k tokens by ~18–35% depending on sequence length distribution, but increases median latency for single-turn interactive flows when warmup/cold policies are naive.
- There is a non-linear interaction: combining moderate compression (brotli-level 4) with medium batching yielded best $/latency tradeoff in our panel workload; extreme compression or extreme batching introduced regressions at p99.

Test harness and config
---
- Harness: inference-harness v0.10 (see linked PR). Client emulation used 300 concurrent virtual users, Poisson arrivals, session length distribution sampled from production-mimic trace: 60% short (<= 40 tokens), 30% medium (40–200 tokens), 10% long (>200 tokens).
- Models: open-llama-7b-quant (float16/4-bit hybrid) on A100-80GB. Kernel selection kept default production knobs.
- Network: two network profiles: LAN (1000 Mbps, 1 ms RTT) and constrained edge (25 Mbps, 30 ms RTT).
- Compression modes: none, gzip-level 6, brotli-level 4. Compression applied to server->client response chunk frames only (not request body).
- Batching: small (max 4), medium (max 12), large (max 32). Batching policy: dynamic window with 20ms max wait.
- Measurements: p50/p95/p99 wall-clock per-response, mean CPU util (serving threads), GPU token throughput (tokens/s), network bytes transferred, estimated $/1k tokens (using internal cost model: GPU minutes + egress + CPU).

Key numeric results (selected slices)
---
Note: numbers are median of three runs; variability +/- 3–8% across runs. All $/1k are relative to baseline (no compression, small batch = 1.00).

1) LAN profile (low network bottleneck)
- baseline (none, small): p50 120ms, p95 380ms, p99 920ms, tokens/s 4200, $/1k = 1.00
- gzip-level6, small: p50 125ms (+4%), p95 385ms (+1%), p99 940ms (+2%), tokens/s 4150, $/1k = 1.02
- brotli-l4, small: p50 123ms, p95 382ms, p99 960ms (+4%), tokens/s 4120, $/1k = 1.03
- none, medium: p50 170ms (+42%), p95 420ms (+11%), p99 990ms (+8%), tokens/s 5200 (+24%), $/1k = 0.83
- brotli-l4, medium: p50 175ms, p95 425ms, p99 1010ms, tokens/s 5100, $/1k = 0.86

2) Constrained edge (bandwidth-bound)
- baseline (none, small): p50 220ms, p95 880ms, p99 1800ms, tokens/s 2700, $/1k = 1.00
- gzip-level6, small: p50 180ms (-18%), p95 610ms (-31%), p99 1400ms (-22%), tokens/s 3000, $/1k = 0.95
- brotli-l4, small: p50 165ms (-25%), p95 520ms (-41%), p99 1200ms (-33%), tokens/s 3200, $/1k = 0.92
- none, medium: p50 260ms (+18%), p95 720ms (-18%), p99 1600ms (-11%), tokens/s 4200 (+55%), $/1k = 0.74
- brotli-l4, medium: p50 240ms, p95 600ms, p99 1350ms, tokens/s 4000, $/1k = 0.77

Observed patterns and interpretation
---
- Network-bound wins: On constrained links, compression materially helps client-observed latency because transfer time dominates for long responses. Brotli at moderate level outperforms gzip in bytes reduction vs CPU cost for our runtime.
- CPU contention risk: When CPU on the host is >70% (observed during large batch + brotli), compression cost (single-threaded encoding per response chunk) inflated p99 tail due to queuing on serving threads. This was most apparent in LAN runs where network wasn't masking CPU cost.
- Batching economy: Larger batches improve GPU utilization and reduce $/1k, but increase median latency for single-turn interactive patterns because dynamic window wait time adds latency. If the product requires sub-150ms median, medium/large batching is not acceptable for short-turn-heavy workloads without fast-path (small-batch preempt).
- Sweet spot: medium batching + brotli-l4 produced a ~20–25% cost reduction while keeping p95 within acceptable bounds for mixed session mixes in edge scenarios. In LAN profile, medium batching alone offered best dollar efficiency but median latency hit was more pronounced.

Rough ASCII sketch (p95 vs $/1k across selected modes)
---
Modes: [none-small, brotli-small, none-medium, brotli-medium]
p95(ms) | $/1k (rel)
----------------------
380     | 1.00   (none-small)
520     | 0.92   (brotli-small)
420     | 0.83   (none-medium)
600     | 0.77   (brotli-medium)

This shows an approximate Pareto frontier: brotli-medium sits left-lower (cheaper but higher p95) for bandwidth-constrained workloads.

Actionable follow-ups
---
- Run CPU-limited experiments with offload: evaluate async compression worker pool to prevent serving-thread blocking (goal: remove p99 regression while preserving bandwidth savings).
- Prototype preemptible small-batch fast-path: allow short single-turn requests to bypass batch window when required latency SLO defined per route.
- Expand to models with larger context windows and multi-turn heavy flows — compression savings likely grow for >512-token outputs.
- Egress cost sensitivity: run same tests with egress pricing modeled for EU vs US edge regions (different egress rates change cost calculus).

Open questions and notes to self
---
- Does brotli CPU cost scale linearly with size? initial profiling suggests superlinear overhead at extreme response sizes (>4KB) due to internal memory operations. Need microprofiling.
- Should we expose a per-route compression knob in Console with an autosuggest based on historical token lengths and client RTT? Feels useful for Private deployments.
- Make sure to cross-check results with dedicated pools (reserved capacity) vs shared hosted API — preemption and scheduling differences may change interplay.

Appendix: quick instrumentation pointers
---
- Measure total blocking time on serving thread (microsec) while compression runs; sample stack traces to confirm blocking point.
- Track bytes-before/after compression and compress ratio histogram per response-length bucket.
- Capture tail queue depth for compression queue if offload prototype implemented.

End of sketch.

(Notes: share with eng-platform and infra; this is roadmap input for optimize/product egress-speedup initiative.)
